lead: A continuous signal can be replaced by a list of numbers if it has no frequency above f_max and we sample faster than twice f_max. The samples keep all the information, and a low-pass filter turns them back into a smooth waveform. This is the bridge from continuous-time to discrete-time processing: phone audio, ECG recorders, digital control and payment logs all store finite samples instead of continuous voltage. Sampling too slowly loses information, a failure studied in 5.2.
prereq: You need: Fourier transform, sinc spectrum and ideal filters (see Unit 3, Fourier Series and Fourier Transform); impulse and standard signals (see Unit 1, Classification of Signals and Systems).

sections.h3: The sampling theorem and its numbers

blocks.text: A signal is band-limited when its Fourier transform is zero above f<sub>max</sub>, the highest frequency in hertz. Sample it at instants nT<sub>s</sub>, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... and T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds. The sampling rate is f<sub>s</sub> = 1/T<sub>s</sub> samples per second, also called hertz. The sampling theorem says: if f<sub>s</sub> > 2 f<sub>max</sub>, the samples x(nT<sub>s</sub>) determine x(t) exactly. The number 2 f<sub>max</sub> is the Nyquist rate. The number f<sub>s</sub>/2 is the Nyquist frequency, the highest frequency a sampler at f<sub>s</sub> can represent. The inequality is strict. At f<sub>s</sub> = 2 f<sub>max</sub>, a sinusoid sitting exactly at f<sub>max</sub> is sampled at the same phase every period, so its amplitude and phase cannot be recovered. Some syllabi call the result the Nyquist–Shannon or Whittaker–Shannon theorem.

blocks.where: f<sub>s</sub> is the sampling rate in Hz; T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds; f<sub>max</sub> is the highest frequency in the signal in Hz; 2 f<sub>max</sub> is the Nyquist rate in Hz; f<sub>s</sub>/2 is the Nyquist frequency in Hz.

sections.h3: Impulse-train model and the repeated spectrum

blocks.text: Multiply x(t) by an impulse train p(t) = Σ δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>). The product is the sampled signal. Each impulse carries one sample value as its area. In frequency, the impulse train has lines at multiples of f<sub>s</sub>. Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency, so the spectrum of the samples is a sum of shifted copies of X(f).
x<sub>s</sub>(t) = x(t) p(t) = Σ x(nT<sub>s</sub>) δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>)
blocks.where: x<sub>s</sub>(t) is the sampled signal; x(nT<sub>s</sub>) is the sample value at time nT<sub>s</sub>; δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>) is a unit impulse at t = nT<sub>s</sub>; the sum runs over all integers n.
X<sub>s</sub>(f) is the spectrum of the samples; X(f) is the original spectrum; f<sub>s</sub> is the sampling rate in Hz; T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds; k runs over all integers.

blocks.text: The original spectrum X(f) is copied at k fs = 0, ±fs, ±2fs, ... and every copy is scaled by 1/Ts. Sketch: draw X(f) from −fmax to fmax, then repeat it every fs hertz. If fs > 2 fmax, the copies do not overlap. The empty gap between the baseband copy and its neighbours is the guard band. If copies overlap, high frequencies fold down as aliasing; see 5.2.

An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and gain T<sub>s</sub> selects the baseband copy and removes all other copies. The gain T<sub>s</sub> cancels the 1/T<sub>s</sub> scaling in X<sub>s</sub>(f), so the output has the original amplitude. In time, the same operation is ideal interpolation: each sample is multiplied by a sinc pulse centred at its sampling instant, and the pulses add to rebuild the smooth signal.
H(f) = T<sub>s</sub> for |f| < f<sub>s</sub>/2, and H(f) = 0 outside
blocks.where: H(f) is the reconstruction filter frequency response; T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds; f<sub>s</sub>/2 is the cutoff frequency in Hz.
sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu) and sinc(0) = 1; x(nT<sub>s</sub>) are the samples; T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds; the sum runs over all integers n.

blocks.text: This is an ideal formula. Real filters have a transition band, and a sample-and-hold circuit attenuates high frequencies. The band-pass sampling case is in 5.3.

figure.caption: The sampler at 1 kHz turns the 450 Hz band-limited signal into samples 1 ms apart; the ideal filter with 500 Hz cutoff and gain T_s rebuilds it.

spec.title: Sampling and ideal reconstruction
spec.aria: A 450 Hz band-limited signal enters a sampler clocked at 1 kHz, giving samples 1 ms apart, and an ideal 500 Hz low-pass filter with gain T_s rebuilds the signal.

examples.question: A voltage x(t) = 3 cos(2π·200t) + 2 cos(2π·450t) volts is sampled at f_s = 1000 Hz. Find f_max, the Nyquist rate, T_s, and the ideal reconstruction filter cutoff. Check whether the spectral copies overlap and state the guard band.
steps: Each cosine has frequency equal to the number multiplying t inside 2π(...). The two frequencies are 200 Hz and 450 Hz, so f_max = 450 Hz.
Nyquist rate = 2 f_max = 2 × 450 Hz = 900 Hz. The actual rate is 1000 Hz, and 1000 Hz > 900 Hz, so the strict sampling condition is met.
The reconstruction filter cutoff is f_s/2 = 1000/2 = 500 Hz. Its passband gain must be T_s.
Sampled-spectrum copies are centred at k f_s = 0, ±1000, ±2000, ... Hz. The baseband copy has components at 200 Hz and 450 Hz. The closest component from the upper copy is 1000 − 450 = 550 Hz.
The gap is 550 Hz − 450 Hz = 100 Hz. No copy overlaps the baseband, so ideal reconstruction returns x(t).
examples.answer: f_max = 450 Hz, Nyquist rate = 900 Hz, T_s = 0.001 s (1 ms), filter cutoff = 500 Hz, lowest upper-copy component = 550 Hz, and guard band = 100 Hz; sampling at 1000 Hz is safe.
examples.check:
fs = 1000.0
f1 = 200.0
f2 = 450.0
fmax = max(f1, f2)
nyquist_rate = 2 * fmax
Ts = 1 / fs
cutoff = fs / 2
lowest_upper = fs - fmax
guard = lowest_upper - fmax
print(fmax)
print(nyquist_rate)
print(Ts)
print(cutoff)
print(lowest_upper)
print(guard)

traps: Nyquist rate is 2 f_max in Hz; Nyquist frequency is f_s/2 in Hz. They are not the same number.
Do not drop the T_s gain of the reconstruction filter; without it the rebuilt signal is scaled by 1/T_s.
f_s = 2 f_max is not safe for a sinusoid at f_max; use f_s > 2 f_max.
Keep units straight: T_s in seconds, f_s in hertz, and 1 ms = 0.001 s.
Examiners often ask for the guard band: lowest upper-copy frequency minus f_max.

quiz.q: Define Nyquist rate and Nyquist frequency.
quiz.a: For f_max = 450 Hz and f_s = 1000 Hz: Nyquist rate = 900 Hz; Nyquist frequency = 500 Hz.

quiz.q: Why is f_s > 2 f_max written with a strict inequality?
quiz.a: At equality, a sinusoid at f_max is sampled at one phase, so its amplitude and phase are lost.

quiz.q: x(t) = 5 cos(2π·300t) is sampled at 800 Hz. Is it safe? Give T_s and cutoff.
quiz.a: f_max = 300 Hz; Nyquist rate = 600 Hz; 800 > 600 so safe. T_s = 1/800 = 1.25 ms; cutoff = 400 Hz.

quiz.q: A 450 Hz component is sampled at 1200 Hz. Find the lowest upper-copy frequency and the guard band.
quiz.a: Copy at 1200 Hz; 1200 − 450 = 750 Hz; guard band = 750 − 450 = 300 Hz.

quiz.q: What do the cutoff and gain of the ideal reconstruction filter do?
quiz.a: Cutoff f_s/2 selects the baseband copy; gain T_s cancels the 1/T_s spectrum scaling.

quiz.q: At f_s = 1000 Hz, give T_s in ms and the reconstruction cutoff.
A signal has 200 Hz and 450 Hz components and is sampled at 900 Hz. Is exact reconstruction guaranteed?
quiz.a: No. Nyquist rate is 900 Hz and the inequality is strict; the 450 Hz component sits at f_s/2 and cannot be recovered in amplitude and phase.

beyond: Not for the exam. Audio codecs and software-defined radios choose f_s from the band of interest and use steep digital filters before downsampling. Medical imaging and vibration monitoring use the same theorem to set recorder rates. Newer work in compressive sensing samples fewer values when the signal is sparse, and sigma-delta converters trade speed for high resolution. Search next: Nyquist criterion, sinc interpolation, oversampling, compressive sensing.
